**(p-40) Surat an-Najm**

Its purpose is the censure of desire (*hawa*), because it produces misguidance and blindness through inclining toward this world, which is the abode of turbidity and affliction, of transience and annihilation, and the praise of knowledge, because it yields guidance through turning toward the Hereafter, which is the abode of permanence, in happiness or in misery. It also exhorts to following the Prophet (ﷺ) in his warning, which Surat Qaf made clear, Surat adh-Dhariyat confirmed, and Surat at-Tur made occur and specified, as it is followed in his good tidings. For his knowledge is the knowledge, since he does not speak out of desire, neither in explicit statement nor in its explanation, because all of it is from Allah, who possesses the attributes of perfection. Therefore there must be a raising of creation to Him and their gathering before Him, so that His wisdom may appear in the utmost manifestation. Thus He raises the people of purification and manifestation, lowers the people of wickedness, and exposes everyone who adorns himself with falsehood and displays evils. This is indicated by its name, an-Najm (The Star), from reflecting on the oath and its answer and what is arranged in it of the "stars" of the Book. (In the name of Allah) who encompasses the attributes of perfection, so His messenger can only be one endowed with perfection. (The Most Gracious) who encompasses existent things with the attribute of beauty. (The Most Merciful) who singles out the people of His love for rescue from misguidance and guidance to what He is pleased with of qualities and righteous deeds.

* *

When the previous surah (at-Tur) ended with the command to the Prophet (ﷺ) to glorify and praise (his Lord), and that command was a creative command (*takwin*, bringing into being) and not a legal obligation (*taklif*), so it would certainly take effect, and that came after they had spoken about the Prophet (ﷺ), claiming he was a soothsayer, a sorcerer, and a madman, and (p-41) since that had a connection with the devils, and the devils were kept apart from the Qur'an by being pelted with meteors from the stars, as the last of the poets explained, this surah opens with exhortation to be guided by his guidance, to draw inference from his indication, and to follow his path. Since among that was his glorifying with praise at the setting of the stars, it swore at the beginning of this surah by the star in a more general manner than what was at the end of that one. It expressed itself with a phrase that conveys its ascent and rising, for no single planet sets in the western horizon without rising from the eastern horizon in a counterpart to it, because of the lofty expression and pure remembrance that occur at that time. Along with this is the wondrous craftsmanship indicating the oneness of its Originator, the adornment of the heaven in which is what you are promised, and the guarding against the rebellious devils, preserving the stars of the Book and guidance by it in religion and in this world, and other wisdoms known to the wise. So He, exalted is He, said: ﴿By the star﴾, that is, this kind of star of the sky, or the Qur'an, because it was revealed in installments, scattered (they call scattering "tanjim", revealing in installments), or the plant. Al-Baghawi said: the star was called a star because of its rising, and every rising thing is a star.

﴿When it descends﴾, that is, sets to disappear, or to pelt the devils when they eavesdrop, as Ikrimah narrated from Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with both of them), if the intended meaning is the celestial star. Then in it is worship, seeking forgiveness, and supplication to the Mighty King at dawn. Or it ascended, and by it the worshipper, the reciter, and the traveler are guided, for it is said: *hawa yahwi hawiyyan* with a fatha means it fell, and with a damma means it rose and ascended. Or the angel descended with it for raising up and for distancing, if the intended meaning is the Qur'an, because of the blessings that come from it in religion and this world, the expansion of the breasts, and the awareness of the wonders of what is decreed. Or it fell flat upon the earth or rose above it, if the intended meaning is the plant, because of its strange craftsmanship and majestic measure, which indicates the comprehensive power, the perfection of knowledge, and the sole possession of dominion and absolute self-sufficiency.

When He had sworn by this magnificent oath, He answered it with His words, using the past tense to negate what they had accused him of. This also makes what came before prophethood easy to understand, so that what came after it is understood a fortiori: ﴿Your companion has not strayed﴾, meaning he did not deviate from the straight path (sawa' al-mahajja, "the right way") that leads to the intended goal. That is, he never once did the deeds of those who go astray. Therefore, the Qur'an could not have been something he invented, nor did he ever act like madmen or anyone else of the kind they had accused him of. As for ﴿And He found you lost﴾ [al-Duha: 7], the intended meaning there is "not knowing." He expressed it with the word "companion" even though "companionship" is more indicative of the intended meaning, since it draws them toward it, makes them favour it, and shames them for accusing him regarding his warning, when they know the goodness of his customs, the purity of his character, and his conduct. So He said: ﴿Your companion﴾, meaning in his warning to you about the Resurrection, so there is no ground for you to accuse him.

Since guidance may be accompanied by an inclination that does not bring the one who reaches it closer to the goal, even though some kind of defect may arise in nearness or the like, the intention may be with something unsuitable. So He said: ﴿Nor has he erred﴾, meaning he did not incline even slightly, and his aim was never something evil. He is protected from its causes, which are the misguidance of the devils and other things. God, glory be to Him, repelled this from our Prophet ﷺ. As for the rest of the prophets, they repelled it from themselves: ﴿There is no misguidance in me﴾ [al-A'raf: 61], ﴿There is no folly in me﴾ [al-A'raf: 67], and the like. This is what al-Qushayri said.

Since guidance may sometimes coincide by chance, He said: ﴿Nor does he speak⁠ ﴾, i.e., his speech does not go beyond his mouth at any time, neither presently nor in the future, as speech arising ﴿from desire﴾, i.e., from his own inclination, like the soothsayers (kuhhān) whose falsehood outweighs their truth, and the poets and others. ﴿And he did not fabricate this Qur'an from himself⁠ ﴾.

Al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on Surah 53, verse 4:

When Allah, glorified is He, emphasized this within Himself by stressing it, to declare Him free of what was attributed to Him, this was a prime occasion for the question about the origin of what he (the Prophet) had uttered, so He answered with restriction (ḥaṣr), and the verse is more explicit and more effective in repelling their extreme denial, and He said: ﴿It is not﴾, i.e., he does not, ﴿but﴾, i.e., what he speaks of from the Qur'an and its explanation, and all his sayings, actions and states, its explanation, ﴿a revelation revealed﴾, i.e., from Allah, exalted is He. He emphasized it with His saying ﴿that is revealed﴾, i.e., its revelation is renewed to him from Us time after time. It is also possible that he ﷺ exercised ijtihad (independent juristic reasoning); then when his ijtihad settled on something, it was revealed to him that you have indeed hit the truth. Moreover, He, glorified is He, had permitted him to exercise ijtihad through revelation, and whoever refers what he exercises ijtihad upon back to what has been revealed to him is free of whim (hawa).

Abu Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr said in his Burhan: When Allah, glorified is He, cut off their attachment with His saying "a sorcerer, a poet, a madman" — along with what he is actually (in their claims) of what they knew does not stand on a leg — but it is the condition of one who is confounded and silenced to rest upon whatever is available to him, even if it does not avail him, Allah, glorified is He, followed with His oath to declare free His Prophet and His chosen one from His creation what the weak ones invented and imagined about him. So He said, exalted is He: ﴿By the star when it sets﴾ [al-Najm: 1] ﴿Your companion has not strayed, nor has he erred﴾ [al-Najm: 2]. Then Allah, glorified is He, followed this oath with an expansion of the state of His nearness to him, peace be upon him, and His drawing him close, and his receiving what he receives from his Lord, and his great station with Him. In displaying that, He stirs them, exalted and majestic is He, reminds them, and rebukes them for the evil of their conduct, with gentleness and by summoning them to a generous Bountiful One, so He said, exalted is He: ﴿Have you considered al-Lat and al-'Uzza﴾ [al-Najm: 19]. The verses were joined around these aims, leading to the announcement of His exclusive oneness, glorified is He, in creating, subduing, honoring and avenging, none sharing with Him in any of that, so He said: ﴿And that to your Lord is the final return﴾ [al-Najm: 42] ﴿And that it is He who makes laugh and makes weep﴾ [al-Najm: 43]. When He made that clear, He said: ﴿So which of the favors of your Lord would you dispute?﴾ [al-Najm: 55], i.e., in which blessing do you doubt, or by which sign do you deny? Then He said: ﴿This is a warner of the warnings of old﴾ [al-Najm: 56]. And if this is the case for him, peace be upon him... then the condition of those who deny him is the condition of those who denied others. End quote.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 53, verse 5:

Since the revelation was manifest through the mediation of the angel (malak), the listener yearned to know an explanation of that, so He said, explaining it by its attributes, because that is more magnificent with respect to Him and higher in its rank: ﴿He taught him﴾, i.e., the revelation that came to you, your companion, with it, ﴿One mighty in power﴾. Will you not marvel at these surging seas by which he has surpassed you, while he is unlettered? For his teacher is with this attribute which he has, to the extent that he carries out everything that Allah commanded him with.

﴿Possessor of strength﴾: that is, of firm resolve, with great power and capacity to carry out what he has been commanded and the ability to bear it, in every state of vigor and vehemence. It is as if he were a temperament in which vehemence predominates. He is difficult to deal with and persists in his course in one manner, with an intensity beyond description. He does not turn in any way toward anything other than what he was commanded. He is in utmost sincerity, his powers are united, his affairs are firmly established, and his resolve is unyielding. There is no weakness in him through which he might cease to be so. Among what he was given of strength and power is the capacity to take on forms. To all of this He alluded by what follows from it, in the words ﴿so he stood firm﴾: that is, he stood upright and balanced with the utmost of his strength (p-٤٥) in his most perfect state, in the form in which he was created.

Ṭhe translation follows.

﴿Wa-huwa﴾ (and he): that is, while the state was that Jibril (peace be upon him) [was there]. Some have allowed that the detached pronoun refers to the Prophet (ﷺ), meaning: Jibril (peace be upon him) stood beside him ﴿bi-al-ufuq al-a'la﴾ (at the highest horizon): that is, the direction which is the utmost point in height and excellence among the heavens, suited to the condition of this standing. This was when the Prophet (ﷺ) saw him sitting on a throne between heaven and earth, having filled the horizon.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 53, verse 8:

When closeness to the Divine Presence (al-hadrah al-ilahiyyah), which is the place prepared for receiving revelation, is of a height and greatness beyond description, he indicated this with the particle of delay, saying: ﴿Then﴾, that is, after that great elevation, ﴿he drew near﴾, that is, Jibril, peace be upon him, drew near to the Most Holy Presence, a nearness of increase in honour, not a nearness of distance. Every nearness that comes from Him, glorified is He, although He is exalted above distance, occurs in two ways: a nearness to every existent from His own essence, and a nearness of guardianship (qurb wilayah), such that He is the hearing and sight of the existent, in the sense that he hears and sees only what pleases Him. Ibn Burjan indicated this. So he took the revelation which he had been permitted to take at that time. ﴿Then he came down﴾ after that, from God, as a messenger to your companion, that is, it was sent down to him with a descent in which he was like one lowering himself to him by a rope, so he reached him without being separated from his station on the highest horizon, because of the strength and firmness he possessed. Al-Baydawi said: For tadalli is a letting-oneself-down combined with attachment, like the hanging of a fruit.

﴿And he was﴾ in nearness to your companion, in the view of whoever among you sees him, ﴿within the measure of﴾, that is, at a distance equal to ﴿two bow-lengths﴾ of your bows. Al-Razi said in *al-Lawami'*: that is, such that the bowstring of the bow would span twice. From Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: the *qaws* is the *dhira'* (forearm-length) in the dialect of Azd Shanu'a. Ibn Burjan said: "*qab* of the two bows" is what lies between the two ends (of the bow). It was also said: what lies between the grip and the bowstring. ﴿Or nearer﴾, meaning that the observer among you, if he saw him, would hesitate, and He said this because of how intensely near to him ﷺ he appeared. Muslim related in the Book of Faith in his *Sahih*, from al-Shaybani, who said: "I asked Zirr ibn Hubaysh about the words of the Most High, ﴿And he was within the measure of two bow-lengths﴾, and he said: Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, told me that the Prophet ﷺ saw Jibril, peace be upon him, and he had six hundred wings."

﴿Then He revealed﴾, i.e., He cast secretly from the speech of Allah, because of this nearness. He followed it with His saying: ﴿to His servant﴾, i.e., the servant of Allah. Its pronoun is left unstated, without prior explicit mention, because what is meant is known from what came earlier at the end of al-Shura: that the speech of Allah comes as revelation through a messenger who conveys it by His permission, glorified is He. The context also suits the use of the pronoun, because the speech is the hidden revelation. He expressed it with distance to indicate that no one else was worthy of this great matter, because he never worshipped anyone other than Allah, and everyone who opposed him had, to some degree, directed worship to other than Him. So he was the most worthy of creation of this description, even though he used to worship Allah in the cave of Hira' and elsewhere. This station, and Allah knows best, was on this reckoning at the beginning of the revelation, when he was at Hira' and was frightened by it, so he ﷺ returned with his shoulders trembling and said: "Wrap me up, wrap me up." He indicated the greatness of what was sent down by His saying: ﴿what He revealed﴾, i.e., it is too exalted to be described, so He summarized for him what He detailed for him afterward. This is the explanation of what is mentioned concerning the apparent pronouns of the expression, although the use of pronouns in all the verbs is not free from ambiguity (p-47) and difficulty. It is possible, on account of the pronoun's capacity to fit what suits it among the apparent meanings, that the pronoun in ﴿drew near﴾ and what follows it refers to Allah, the Exalted. In that case, the "His" in ﴿His servant﴾ becomes clear, as was mentioned in this aspect, that He gave it to Him, glorified is He, because it is not permissible for anyone else.

Al-Bukhari related in the Book of Tawhid, under the chapter "﴿And Allah spoke to Moses directly﴾ [al-Nisa': 164]," from Anas, may Allah be pleased with him, concerning the story of the Night Journey of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ from the Masjid of the Ka'bah, that: "Three men came to him before he was revealed to, while he was sleeping in the Sacred Mosque. The first of them said: 'Which of them is he?' The middle one said: 'He is the best of them.' The last of them said: 'Take the best of them.' That was one night, and he did not see them until they came to him another night, while his heart saw them and his eye slept but his heart did not sleep—and so it is with the prophets: their eyes sleep but their hearts do not sleep. They did not speak to him until they carried him and placed him by the well of Zamzam, and Jibril, peace be upon him, took charge of him. Jibril split what was between his chest and his lower throat until he had finished with his chest and belly, and he washed it with the water of Zamzam with his own hand until he had purified his inside. Then he brought a golden basin containing gold-colored light, filled with faith and wisdom, and he filled his chest and his la'adid—meaning the veins of his throat—with it. Then he closed it up and ascended with him to the lowest heaven. He knocked on one of its doors, and the people of the heaven called out: 'Who is this?' He said: 'Jibril.' They said: 'Who is with you?' He said: 'With me is Muhammad.' They said: 'Has he been sent for?' He said: 'Yes.' They said: 'Welcome to him'—and in welcome and ease—" Then he mentioned his ascent through the seven heavens, and that when he reached the seventh heaven, He raised him above that to a height known only to Allah, until he came to the Lote Tree of the Utmost Boundary (Sidrat al-Muntaha). The Compeller, the Lord of Might, drew near, and He descended toward him, so he was at a distance of two bow-lengths or nearer. Then He revealed to him what He reveals, fifty prayers. He mentioned Moses's counsel, peace be upon him, in asking for a reduction, until they became five, each one counting as ten. The Compeller, the Lord of Might, drew near in this aspect, and He is the Lord of Might."

This is most excellent when you combine it with what comes in this aspect, transmitted from Ja'far al-Sadiq, may Allah be pleased with him. The meaning then is that when he ﷺ rose to the highest horizon and reached a limit beyond which a created being cannot ascend, the Creator, glorified is He, descended to him. For this reason the expression used "then" (thumma), meaning that He, glorified is He, descended to him with a descent in which the true measure of His rank in height and greatness cannot be grasped. Then He descended, then He descended further.

Since the expression may perhaps give rise to an idea unbefitting Him, he ﷺ negated it by what is in the narration of specifying the expression with the name "the Compeller." It is thus known that He brought him near in a manner befitting Him, and He called that "drawing near." So drawing near and descending are an illustration of what reached him from Him, glorified is He, to His servant Muhammad ﷺ with the utmost ease, facility and gentleness, together with his connection to the holy presences. The expression "descent" conveys height, just as He used the term "descending" each night to the lowest heaven as a metaphor for answering supplication by opening the doors (p-49) of the heaven, as we have related in the Juz' of al-'Ayshi from the hadith of 'Uthman ibn Abi al-'As, may Allah be pleased with him. This is an illustration by what we know of the state of kings: one of them descends from his throne to come to his close attendants, and opens his door to those nearest to him, and each step he descends, the permission becomes more general, until it reaches general permission for all people. This is the knowledge of the addressees that this is by way of illustration, with one who needs these degrees. As for He who is free of all need, for Him is the highest likeness, and nothing resembles Him, and nothing is like Him. Further clarification of this is found in the "Qur'an of Dawn" in Surat Subhan. Al-Qadi 'Iyad said in al-Shifa' what in summary is that these pronouns refer to the Prophet ﷺ. He said: Ja'far ibn Muhammad—meaning al-Sadiq ibn al-Baqir—said: "His Lord brought him near until he was as two bow-lengths." He also said: "The modality ceased from the nearness. Do you not see how Jibril, peace be upon him, was veiled from his nearness, while Muhammad ﷺ drew near to what He deposited in his heart of knowledge and faith, and so he descended by the tranquility of his heart to what brought him near, and doubt and suspicion departed from his heart." Ja'far also said: "Nearness to Allah, exalted is He, has no limit, and nearness for servants is by limits." End of quotation.

In that case the pronoun in ﴿rose﴾ refers to him ﷺ, and the meaning is: from Jibril's teaching him there resulted his ﴿rising﴾, i.e., the balance of his knowledge, to a degree no other creature reached in knowledge and acquisition concerning the dominion and the kingdom of the unseen, while he was at the highest horizon on the night of the Ascension. His ﴿descent﴾ is a metaphor for his arrival through a great means, the means carrying the one who descends. The expression is clear regarding descent from a height, together with not being separated from it, lest it give the impression that the direction of height is specific to Him, glorified is He, to the exclusion of the other directions. From this is the saying: "The closest a servant is to his Lord is when he is prostrating." Likewise it was said regarding the indication in "Do not prefer me over Yunus ibn Matta." And among the very fine points is that the alif of "tadalla" (descended), which changed from a ya', in this aspect be a substitute for a lam, so that it becomes from tadallul, which is familiarity and openness out of confidence in love. It is said: "He became familiar with him (tadallala 'alayhi)," i.e., he was open and confident in his love, so he went to excess with him. His openness ﷺ in that state is the excess of the abundance of his requests and his intercession for his community. By this it became manifest to the world of witness that he is the most merciful of creation, just as it was known to the world of the unseen. Thus there resulted an increase in his drawing near, until he was at a distance of two bow-lengths or nearer. The presentation of this speech in these pronouns, which bear these aspects without an apparent word that specifies the intended meaning, suits that state, for it was a state of the unseen, concealment and veiling, and knowledge in it was vast. The arrangement of pronouns in this way increases the possibility of the speech bearing these aspects, so that knowledge expands, while there is no aspect in it that leads to confusion in religion, nor to weakness of meaning, nor of composition, nor any gap for knowledge. And Allah knows best.

When this discourse established the nearness to the Prophet ﷺ of the one who was revealed to, on both interpretations, it confirmed that nearness in a manner that conveys sight. So He said: ﴿The heart did not lie about what it saw.﴾ That is, the heart, which is at the peak of intelligence and perception, ﴿did not lie about what it saw﴾. That is, at the time of the eye's seeing, the heart was present. It is not merely a sight of the eye, in which attributing error would be possible because the heart was absent from it. Al-Qushayri said, in meaning: the heart of Muhammad ﷺ did not lie about what his eye saw, but rather he saw it in the description which he knew before he saw it, so his knowledge was *haqq al-yaqin* (the certainty of certainty).

In Sahih Muslim, on the authority of Abu Dharr, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "I asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, 'Did you see your Lord?' He said, 'It is light; how could I see Him?'"

Also in Sahih Muslim, on the authority of Masruq, that he said to Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, when she denied the sight: "Did not Allah, the Exalted, say: ﴿And he certainly saw him at the clear horizon﴾ [al-Takwir: 23] and ﴿And he certainly saw him in another descent﴾ [al-Najm: 13]?" She said: "I am the first of this community to ask the Messenger of Allah ﷺ about that, and he said: 'It was only Jibril, peace be upon him. I did not see him in his created form except these two times. I saw him descending from the sky, his great form filling what is between the sky and the earth.'"

Al-Baghawi said: A group of scholars held that he saw Him. Some of them said: "He placed his sight in his heart." Then it is narrated from Sahih Muslim, on the authority of Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that he said: "He saw Him with his heart, twice." A group of scholars held that he saw Him with his eye, and this is the view of Anas, may Allah be pleased with him.

Ibn Burjan said, in meaning: sleep and swooning are among the signs of Allah concerning the meeting with Allah, and they are preludes to that, and every reality has a truth that precedes it, like the *ashrat al-sa'a* (portents of the Hour). The *isra'* (the night journey), even if it was neither death, nor swooning, nor sleep according to the most apparent view, has nonetheless departed from the observations of this world to the observations of the highest horizon. So sight there is not to be denied. The *isra'* is a state other than the state of this world; rather, it is one of the states of the Hereafter and the unseen world. And Allah is the Guide.

Now that this has been established to the utmost degree of establishment, and since it was the very point of their denial, He said, as a consequence of that: ﴿Will you then dispute with him over what he sees?﴾ That is, will you draw out from him, through your argument with him, doubt about what he told you, while there is no doubt in it? He expressed it with the form of mutual action (mufa'alah) in the reading of the majority, as opposed to Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Ya'qub, to indicate their striving to cast doubt upon him. It derives from mara (مرى) al-shay', meaning he extracted it; and mara al-naqah (مرى الناقة), meaning he stroked her udder, so that amra (أمرى) meant her milk flowed. Al-miryah (المرية), with kasrah or dammah, means doubt and disputation. ﴿over what he sees﴾: in a manner where the heart and the sight correspond, and that is of a kind in which it is not customary for doubt to enter nor for it to accept disputation. He further clarified the matter by depicting the past situation with the present tense, indicating that just as he did not doubt, the matter was not confused for him; rather, it is as if he is now looking.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 53, verse 13:

When a thing is at its strongest when the sight is weary, and when the heart is in a state of utmost presence it becomes more possible; and when this is repeated, the hopes of [the disbelievers] for disputing it are cut off, [Allah] said, emphasizing on account of their denial: ﴿And he certainly saw him﴾, that is, Allah the Exalted, or Jibril (upon him be peace), in his true form. Muslim related in al-Iman, "from Abdullah ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both), who said, [concerning] ﴿The heart did not lie about what it saw﴾ [al-Najm: 11] and ﴿And he certainly saw him in another descent﴾, he said: 'He saw him with his heart twice.'" Ibn Burjan made the Isra' (the Night Journey) twice: the first with the heart, in advance, and this one with the eye.

When that could not be achieved except by a descent that crosses the distances of remoteness, which are the veils, so that he would be in a position where a human being could see him, [Allah] expressed it with His saying: ﴿descent﴾, and it is put in the accusative as an adverb of time, because the verb-form (fa'lah) carries the meaning of "a single occurrence" ﴿another﴾, that is, so that the matter would be complete for him, once in the world of generation and corruption and another time in the most exalted, most pure place. He specified the time by specifying the place, so he said:

﴿At the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary﴾, i.e., the tree that is like the lote-tree (sidr), at which the knowledge of all creatures ends, and to which there ascends what rises from below and there descends what comes down from above, so that it is received there. And that, God knows best, was on the night of the Isra' (night journey) in the thirteenth year of prophethood, shortly before the Hijra, after an ascent through the mi'raj (ascent) of perfections, through years according to the number of the heavens and the distances between them, until he reached a limit where the scratching of the pens could be heard. And he magnified it with his saying:

"Near it" – that is, near the lote-tree of the boundary – "is the Garden of Refuge" – the one which, in truth, has no other refuge beside it, since nothing can be compared to it in its greatness. And he added to its glorification with his saying:

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 53, verse 16:

﴿When that which covers the lote-tree covered it﴾. That is, it covers it, envelops it, and [the lote-tree] bears fruit of it? [It is covered] with the bed-cloth of gold, the green rafraf (cushions), the angels, the lote-berries (nabq), and other things. Indeed, al-ghashw (covering) is the nabq, and ﴿what covered it﴾ is something you cannot bear to describe, being of such a kind that it nearly cannot be counted. To this the Prophet (ﷺ) alludes in the hadith: "It was covered [by] ... Indeed, I do not know what it is, and none of the creation of Allah is able to describe it," or as he (ﷺ) said. [Allah] emphasized the seeing and confirmed it, beginning a new statement with His saying:

ما زاغَ ﴿Mā zāgha﴾ — "it did not swerve": that is, it did not incline even slightly. ﴿Al-baṣar﴾ — "the sight": that is, the sight that no created being has a more perfect sight than it. So it did not fall short in looking at what it was permitted to look at, nor did it exceed that. ﴿Wa mā ṭaghā﴾ — "nor did it transgress": that is, it did not go beyond the limit into what it was not permitted. This is despite the fact that that world is strange to the children of Adam, and in it are wonders that bewilder the beholder. Rather, he possessed true chastity, balanced between greed and renunciation, in accordance with the most perfect laws of justice; so he affirmed what he saw as it truly was. As al-Suhrawardi (Shihab al-Din al-Suhrawardi, author of ʿAwarif al-Maʿarif) said at the beginning of the thirty-second chapter of his ʿAwarif: "God, exalted is He, informed of the goodness of his adab (courtesy) in the Presence through this verse, and this is one of the abstruse subtleties of adab, which was specific to the Messenger of God (ﷺ)."

(p-54) When they denied the Night Journey (al-Isra') with a denial that they had never shown toward anything else, He increased its emphasis in a way that covers everything else, and so He said: ﴿He certainly saw﴾, that is, he saw, by reason of what We had qualified him for of prophethood, a seeing that penetrated to the inner realities and did not stop at the outward appearances, ﴿of the signs of his Lord﴾, that is, the One who did good to him with what no one before him had reached and no one after him will reach, and whoever claims that is an unbeliever, ﴿the greatest﴾. Among that is what he saw in the heavens of the prophets, upon him and upon them be prayers and peace, indicating through each thing a matter that is subtle and sublime and a state that is noble.

Abu al-Qasim al-Suhayli (al-Suhayli) said in al-Rawd al-Unuf: "What I say about this is that the source of his understanding lies in the science of interpretation (ta'bir, the interpretation of dreams), for it belongs to the science of prophethood. The people of ta'bir say: whoever sees a prophet in his true form in a dream, his vision signals something resembling that prophet's condition, whether in hardship or ease or other matters that have been reported about the prophets in the Qur'an and the hadith. The hadith of the Night Journey took place in Makkah, and Makkah is God's sanctuary and place of safety, and its inhabitants are God's neighbours, because His House is in it. So the first of the prophets whom he (ﷺ) saw was Adam, upon him be prayers and peace, who had been in God's safety and protection, until Iblis, his enemy, expelled him from it. This story resembles the first state of the Prophet (ﷺ), when his enemies expelled him from the sanctuary of God and from the neighbourhood of His House, and that grieved and saddened him, so his story in this respect resembled the story of Adam, upon him be prayers and peace. Yet Adam had the spirits of his offspring, both the righteous and the wicked, presented to him, so he was in the lowest heaven in a position from which he could see both groups, because the spirits of the people of wretchedness do not enter the heavens and their gates are not opened for them, as God the Exalted said. Then in the second heaven he saw Jesus and John, upon them both be prayers and peace, and they are the two who were tested by the Jews. As for Jesus, peace be upon him, the Jews denied him, harmed him and planned to kill him, so God raised him up to Himself. As for John, peace be upon him, they killed him. After the Messenger of God (ﷺ) migrated to Madinah, he entered a second state of testing, and his trial there was with the Jews: they harmed him, backed one another against him, and planned to drop a rock on him to kill him, but God saved him, as He had saved Jesus, peace be upon him, from them. Then they poisoned him in the sheep, and that poisoning kept recurring on him until it cut his aorta, as he said at the time of death. And so they did with the two cousins, John and Jesus, for the mother of John, Ashya', daughter of 'Imran, was the sister of Mary daughter of 'Imran, and their mother was Jannah. As for his meeting with Joseph, peace be upon him, in the third heaven, it signals a third state resembling the state of Joseph, peace be upon him, for Joseph prevailed over his brothers after they had expelled him from among them, so he pardoned them and said: ﴿No blame will be upon you today; God will forgive you﴾ [Yusuf: 92], and the verse continues. Likewise our Prophet (ﷺ) took captive on the day of Badr a number of his relatives who had expelled him, among them his uncle al-'Abbas and his cousin 'Aqil. Some of them he released, and some he accepted ransom from, (p-55) and then after that he prevailed over them on the day of the Conquest, gathered them and said to them: 'I say what my brother Joseph said: ﴿No blame will be upon you today﴾' [Yusuf: 92]. Then his meeting with Idris, peace be upon him, in the fourth heaven, which is the place God called a lofty place, and Idris was the first to whom God gave writing with the pen. That signalled the fourth state, which is the elevation of his station, peace be upon him, to the point that he frightened kings and wrote to them calling them to obey him, until Abu Sufyan, when he was with the king of Rome and the letters of the Prophet (ﷺ) arrived and he saw what he saw of Heraclius's fear, said: 'The affair of the son of Abi Kabshah has become so great that the king of the Banu al-Asfar fears him.' Writing was sent in his name with the pen to all the kings of the earth. Some of them followed him in his religion, like the Negus and the king of Oman, and some made peace with him and gave him gifts and presents, like Heraclius and al-Muqawqis, and some rebelled against him, and God made him prevail over them. So this is a lofty station and writing with the pen, like what Idris, peace be upon him, was given. His meeting in the fifth heaven with Aaron, peace be upon him, who was beloved among his people, signals that Quraysh and all the Arabs loved him after they had hated him. His meeting in the sixth heaven with Moses, peace be upon him, signals a state resembling the state of Moses, peace be upon him, when he was commanded to fight in Syria, and he prevailed over the tyrants who were there, and he brought the children of Israel into the land from which they had come out after the destruction of their enemy. For this reason the Messenger of God (ﷺ) campaigned to Tabuk from the land of Syria and prevailed over the lord of Dumah, (p-57) until he made peace with him on the basis of the jizyah (poll tax) after he had brought him as a captive. He also conquered Makkah, and his companions entered the land from which they had come out. Then his meeting in the seventh heaven with Abraham, peace be upon him, was for two reasons. The first is that he saw him at the Bayt al-Ma'mur (the frequented house), leaning his back against it, and the Bayt al-Ma'mur is the mountains of Makkah, and to it the angels make pilgrimage, just as Abraham, peace be upon him, is the one who built the Ka'bah and called people to the pilgrimage (hajj) to it. The second wisdom is that the last of the states of the Prophet (ﷺ) was his pilgrimage to the Sacred House, and about seventy thousand Muslims performed the pilgrimage with him that year. The vision of Abraham, peace be upon him, according to the people of interpretation (ta'wil, the interpretive reading of symbols) signals the pilgrimage, because he is the one who called to it and raised the foundations of the Ka'bah, which is visited on pilgrimage." Here ends the quotation from al-Suhayli.

This station is the Night Journey and what branches from it, which leads to the highest degree of the purification of monotheism. So He, glorified be He, made its prescribed emblem, which distinguishes between Islam and polytheism, the prayer (salah), which combines the meanings of the religion and comprises all blessings. He made it fifty prayers encompassing all the time, then reduced it to five, without much loss of strength. Then He arranged upon them the reward of the fifty, and raised each prayer offered in congregation (salat al-jama'ah) to twenty-seven prayers, and He favoured the two prayers at the two ends of the day: the dawn prayer, which is two units, and the afternoon prayer, which is four units, by the testimony of the two groups of angels, who record them in the scrolls of each of the two assemblies.

Hamza al-Kirmani said in Jawami' al-Tafsir (Compendia of Exegesis): "He was taken on the Night Journey in the month of Rabi' al-Awwal before the Hijrah, from the house of Umm Hani', may God be pleased with her." Then he related the hadith of the Night Journey in a very wondrous and very lengthy manner.

(p-58) When Allah, glory be to Him, had informed of the uprightness of the path of His Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, in that his message was established by what was revealed to him and by the signs he was shown, through which the right of Allah, glory be to Him, alone to divinity was manifested, He consequently rebuked them for worshipping their objects of worship, in a manner that indicates they are not fit to be worthy of worship. So He said: ﴿Have you considered?﴾ That is, tell me, on account of what I have recited to you of these dazzling signs: have you looked, with the sight of insight into the inner and the outer, at ﴿al-Lat﴾, which was the idol of Thaqif, and ﴿al-'Uzza﴾, which was a tree belonging to Ghatafan? These two were the greatest of their idols, for they used to swear by them.

﴿And Manāt﴾, which is a rock belonging to Hudhayl and Khuzā'ah. He indicates that they regarded it, after the other two, as having lordship (al-rubūbiyyah, lordship over creation) by his saying, pointing through the use of the word "third" and the way it is expressed: ﴿the third, the other﴾. This means that none of them is fit to be worthy of anything, not even to be mentioned. That is, they were not content, in breaching the barrier of reason, with merely multiplying the deity by making it two, so they added a third, which they acknowledged to be of lower rank. Thus the deity, in their view, could be base, and could be bound to descent and lowliness by being female. Al-Razi said in al-Lawāmi': "They made its name feminine, likening it to the angels, according to their claim that they were the daughters of God." End of quote. There is no doubt, for anyone with even minimal knowledge of eloquence (fasāhah), that this interrogative of denunciation, and the expression with "mā" (what) whose nature is bearing children, which is the thing most beloved to a human being, indeed to an animal, does not accord with saying after it anything that implies praise in any respect. Thus the falsehood of what was transmitted through a feeble transmission is made clear: that it was said, when this surah was recited at this place, "Those are the exalted cranes (al-gharānīq al-ʿulā)," and so on to its end. Every Arab knows that this is an extreme of nonsense in this context, so there is no connection between this and this miraculous context in any respect.

(p-59) Since the implied meaning, as the context indicates, is: How can you claim they are gods? Is it so, when your custom is to despise females, [even to the point of] not wanting daughters for yourselves? How then are you content to have them as gods, and to be their worshippers, when they have not sent down to you any revelation, nor sent you any messenger, nor done for anyone among you anything of what We honored Our servant Muhammad (ﷺ) with, nor ever shown you any sign, nor are they even fit for any of that? Rather, they possess no power to harm or benefit. Yet you claimed that they are His daughters, and that jinn-females settled among them are His daughters. You also claimed, along with attributing sonship in general to One who has no need of it and no likeness to it, that He has the inferior of the two kinds [for offspring]. Thus that amounted to one deficiency added to another. Exalted is He, far above having a consort or a son. Therefore you deserved this severe denunciation. And from this meaning, which the context guides to, the falsity of the report of the Gharaniq (the so-called "satanic verses" narration) becomes evident, especially given what follows it in His words: ﴿Is the male for you?﴾, i.e., exclusively for you, ﴿the male⁠﴾, i.e., the superior kind, ﴿and for Him﴾, i.e., alone, ﴿the female⁠﴾, i.e., the inferior kind.

Since the interrogation was a rebuke, He answered their denial with this statement, as a *fadhlakah* (a concluding summary) of their action: ﴿That﴾, that is, this division far from what is right, ﴿since﴾, that is, since you made the daughters for Him and the sons for yourselves, ﴿is an unjust division﴾, that is, oppressive, deficient, and wrong in what is good for the truth, crooked in its purpose and not balanced, in that you assigned to Him what your dislike of it had driven you to bury alive. It is known that the verse is an example of *ihtibak* (a rhetorical device in which one element of a pair is mentioned and its counterpart omitted, and the omitted counterpart is understood from the mentioned one). The mention of its name in the denunciatory style indicates the omission of a denial that they are gods, and the denial of their assigning it to females indicates the omission of what shows that they made them His daughters.

When this denial made clear the falsity of their claim, he confined the true statement to it, saying, in a resumed sentence: ﴿They are not﴾, that is, these idols are not, ﴿but names﴾, that is, they have no realities. So whatever divinity you claim for them, they have of it nothing but names. He emphasised this by saying, explaining: ﴿which you have named﴾, that is, you yourselves invented their naming, and he uprooted their claim from its base, saying: ﴿you and your fathers﴾, that is, not by anything but mere whim. You have never seen from them any sign, nor has any of them ever spoken to you a word you could count. And supposing the devils spoke through their tongues, what sound path have they prescribed for you, what fine or eloquent speech has reached you from them, and what great sign have they shown you? That is the end of the quotation.

Since this made known that God, exalted is He, had not commanded them to any of this, he stated it explicitly, denying that anything they had named points to a proof, and said: ﴿God has not sent down﴾. Earlier, in al-A'raf, he had placed the negative particle for gradual progression, in line with what preceded, and here he used the negation that covers the act itself, whether gradually or otherwise, because the distinguishing feature of the Qur'anic discourse is that it aims at purposes. That suffices for condemning whim, which is the aim of the surah. He said: ﴿God﴾, to whom belong all the attributes of perfection, ﴿has not sent down﴾ ﴿with it﴾, that is, with any right to the names, nor for what you have named them with of divinity. He intensified the negation by saying: ﴿any authority﴾, that is, any proof fit to empower whoever claims it.

Since this all-encompassing negation obliges the opponent to exhaust every ingenuity in producing a proof, in whatever manner, and since these people had become dumbfounded upon hearing these words, finding nothing to say, and it was their duty to return but they did not return, he turned away from them, signalling their utter loss, saying: ﴿They follow only﴾ (p-61) that is, at no time, regarding these idols, with the utmost of their effort, that they are gods, and that they intercede for them or bring them closer to God. ﴿Nothing but conjecture﴾, that is, the utmost of their affair for whoever thinks well of them. Conjecture is the preponderance of one of two possibilities against the will of the one conjecturing.

Since conjecture may sometimes agree with the truth and oppose whim, he said: ﴿and what the souls desire﴾, that is, what they crave. And they, because of their deficiency, never crave anything except what drags them down from the peak of their height to the bottom of their abyss. As for lofty things and the goodness of outcomes, it is only the intellect that yearns for them. Al-Qushayri said: a good opinion of God is not of this category, and the confusion of a person's outcomes upon him is not a path within this sentence. Rather, what is meant is the flawed conjecture about God, His attributes and His rulings.

﴿And indeed﴾, that is, it is strange that they do this while there has already come to them ﴿from their Lord﴾, that is, the One who is good to them, ﴿the guidance﴾, that is, the one perfect in its field, to the true religion, articulated by the Book, articulated by the correct, upon the tongue of the Messenger (ﷺ). Sound judgement requires that whoever sees guidance follows it even if his enemy brings it to him, so how much more when it is brought by one better than him, from one whose goodness towards him has never ceased at all. Since the implied sense was: is it incumbent upon them to abandon their desires and be guided by the guidance of their Lord, to whom they have no sovereignty

The commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 53, verse 24:

﴿Or﴾ do they have what they wish? This was the original wording, but he mentioned the underlying cause that necessitates following desire, so he said: ﴿for man﴾, meaning the one who is intimate with himself, who approves of everything he does and neglects, ﴿has what he wishes﴾, meaning from following what he desires: rank, wealth, long life, a life of ease, and from his disbelief and obstinacy, and from his saying: ﴿And if I am returned to my Lord, I will surely have the best with Him﴾ [Fussilat 41:50].

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 53, verse 25:

(p-62). Since the interrogation is one of denial, the meaning is: "He does not have what he wishes." This is a conclusive proof that he is a subject, subdued by the One to whom the entire command belongs. Therefore He makes the following statement a consequence of it: ﴿So to Allah belongs﴾, i.e., the Greatest King alone. Since the Hereafter (al-Akhira) is the abode of pleasures, the attainment of all hopes, and their deprivation, and since they used to claim, on the supposition that it would be so, that it would grant them everything they wished for, namely the intercession of their gods, their being granted it, their felicity, and the like, He placed His statement ﴿the Hereafter﴾ first. He gives hopes in it only to those who follow His guidance and oppose their desires. ﴿And the first (al-Ula)﴾: He does not give all hopes in it to anyone at all, as is observed. Whoever abandons his desire in this world attains his hopes in the Hereafter, and whoever follows his desire does not reach his aim in this world and is deprived of his hopes in the Hereafter. Therefore He placed it first, not for the sake of the rhyme (fasila), for had it been said "al-Ukhra" it would have suited the rhyme.

The text was read as the commentary's own discussion: "And since the sense is: how many a person you see on earth, although in your apparent view he is in the utmost power, does not attain a quarter of what he wishes, He followed it with His saying, displaying the vastness of His dominion and that He does not care for anyone, indicating abundance: ﴿And how many an angel﴾, that is, one brought near, and He indicated the increase of his nearness by the nobility of his dwelling, so He said: ﴿in the heavens﴾, that is, while they are in honour and nearness, ﴿will not avail﴾, that is, will not suffice, will not fill the need, and will not be enough. And since returning the plural to the state of their gathering is more indicative of greatness, He expressed it with what admits of that, so He said: ﴿their intercession﴾, that is, on behalf of any of the people, ﴿anything﴾. So He restricted the matter and returned it entirely to Him by His saying: ﴿except﴾, and by affirming the preposition He indicated that it is with what God, glory be to Him, limits, not absolutely, so He said: ﴿after He grants permission﴾, that is, enables and wills, ﴿God﴾ (p-٦٣), that is, the One with whom no command whatsoever belongs to anyone at all. He expressed it with "an" and the verb to indicate that there is no generality after the permission for all times; rather that is renewed after the renewal of permission at its time, and before the command: "the gate?" — because of the generality of greatness, by His saying: ﴿for whom He wills﴾, that is, by the renewal of the attachment of His will to him, so that he may be one who is interceded for or one who intercedes.

And since the king may grant permission for intercession while he is unwilling, He said, informing that He is not like those: ﴿and is pleased﴾. Then their intercession avails when they are among those granted permission. All of this is a definitive cutting off of their hopes and of their saying, by mere caprice, that their gods intercede for them. And since He informed of their following of caprice and negated that they should have from that what they wish, He indicated their following of caprice by His saying in the place of "that they":"

"Verily, those who" — He emphasized the warning, indicating that this is a statement of extreme wonder, such that it is hardly believable that a rational person who believes in the Hereafter would say it, given what befell them for their saying that and similar things. With His words: ﴿do not believe﴾, i.e., they neither affirm it nor acknowledge ﴿the Hereafter﴾. For this reason He emphasized His saying: ﴿they name the angels﴾, i.e., each one of them, and they are the messengers of Allah, ﴿with the naming of females﴾, by saying: they are the daughters of Allah, just as the word "banat" (daughters) is used for the female gender in general.

Wa-mā (and the case being that) they have no knowledge of it, that is, of what they named [the angels] by; he intensified the negation with His words: "of knowledge." When He negated their knowledge, the listener became eager to know what moved them to do so, so He said: "in" (they follow nothing but), that is, with the utmost of what can be in that and other matters, "except conjecture" (al-zann).

Since they acted as though they were certain that this would benefit them, He emphasized His statement: "And indeed conjecture," that is, absolutely, in this matter and others. For this reason He used the apparent noun in place of the pronoun, saying "does not avail" in a way that begins any benefit "against the truth" (min al-haqq), that is, the established reality in itself, which is the true nature and essence of a thing, such that conjecture would stand in its place. Conjecture is only expressed in practical matters (al-'amaliyyat), not in matters of knowledge (al-'ilmiyyat), especially the foundational ones (al-usuliyyah), "anything" of benefit concerning anyone among the creatures. For it never leads to certain knowledge of a thing as it is in reality, and so it is prohibited in the foundations of religion (usul al-din), since the aim there is to establish the matter as it actually is. As for the subsidiary rulings (furu'), the one obligated in them is conjecture, but under its permitted condition, which is returning it to the foundations from which it is derived (istinbat), because human beings are unable to attain certainty in all the subsidiary rulings. This is a reminder of his incapacity and his need for God, so that he turns to Him, disclaims his own power and strength, and so that He may reveal to him what he did not know (min al-ahqaf).

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 53, verse 29:

When they, after the coming of the guidance, had persisted in (following) their whims, and this surah was among the first to be revealed while the believers were few, He consequently said: ﴿So turn away from one who turns away from Our remembrance﴾, meaning: whoever turns away (from it) burdens himself with (acting) contrary to what reason and natural disposition call him to, ﴿from Our remembrance﴾, meaning His remembrance of Us, so he turns away from the Reminder which We have sent down, does not attain it, and does not reflect on its meanings. So he does not heed anything he knows, for it is obliterated upon his heart, and even if his intellect were finer than poetry, it will only lead to evil. ﴿So let not your soul go to waste in regret over them﴾ [Fatir: 8], for upon you there is nothing but conveyance (of the message).

Since the one who turns away at one time may turn toward (the truth) at another, He indicated his persistence in an eloquent manner by saying: ﴿And he desires not﴾, meaning at any time whatsoever, ﴿except the worldly life﴾, meaning the present one, so that he aims at it through sensible things like the cattle, blind to its baseness and worthlessness. Then he restated the two clauses of turning away and desiring with His saying:

﴿That﴾, i.e. the matter that has reached the utmost in ignorance and ugliness, ﴿is their extent﴾, i.e. the limit of their reaching and the place their attainment ends. He mocks them with His words ﴿of knowledge﴾, meaning that they have no knowledge, because the eyes of their insight are blind and their mirrors are dense and dark, not disclosing the view of the Hereafter, which is the root of all sciences.

Then he gives the reason for this sentence with His words, emphasizing it to cut off the hope of one who thinks that his preaching and speech might turn anyone back from his error, however much he exerts himself in his affair and in his supplication privately and publicly. It also informs that this is only from Allah. Whoever is preached to by Him, hoping from Him for his faith, is near to being benefited by it, as occurred in the preaching of Mus'ab ibn 'Umayr, may Allah be pleased with him, when Usayd ibn Hudayr and Sa'd ibn Mu'adh, may Allah be pleased with both of them, listened to him in one and the same hour, as is well known. ﴿Indeed your Lord﴾, i.e. the One who has bestowed favor upon you by sending you and otherwise, ﴿He﴾, i.e. alone, ﴿is most knowing of whoever strays from His way﴾, straying persistently. So do not hang your hope on his knowledge reaching beyond this world. He expressed it with "Lord" to indicate that the straying of this man is part of the favor toward him (ﷺ), because if he had entered into his religion he would have corrupted more than he would have reformed, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And they would have hurried through your ranks, seeking to cause you discord, and among you are listeners to them﴾ [al-Tawbah: 47]. That is because he was created with a nature not receptive to good. ﴿And He﴾, i.e. alone, (p-66) ﴿is most knowing of whoever is guided﴾, i.e. outwardly and inwardly.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 53, verse 31:

Since this might give the impression that whoever has gone astray in this state is not in His grip, He said, benefiting from this ambiguity by making clear that He possesses the Most Beautiful Names (al-asma' al-husna) and their requirements in the world. The phrase "والحالُ أنَّهُ لَهُ" ("while the state is that it belongs to Him") is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), or it is a conjunction (ʿatf) with what is implied by its estimate: "So to Allah belongs whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth." ﴿And to Allah belongs﴾, that is, to the Supreme King alone, ﴿whatever is in the heavens﴾ of beings and meanings. This includes the heavens and the earths, since every heaven is within the one that follows it, and the earth is within the heaven. ﴿And whatever is on the earth﴾, and likewise the lands, and all of it is within the Throne, and He is the Lord of the Mighty Throne.

When He commanded him ﷺ to turn away from them, consoled him, and informed him that all of it is in His dominion, so that if He willed He would guide them and end the dispute, but He has wisdoms in that which thoughts are bewildered by, He gave a reason for turning away, as was mentioned earlier in al-Jathiyah in His saying: ﴿Say to those who believe, forgive﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 14], by His saying: ﴿so that He may recompense﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 14], that is, He, glory be to Him, will punish, being sufficient for you in what concerns you of that. It is also possible that the estimate is: Just as He, glory be to Him, is the owner of that, He is also its King, so that He may judge the recompense of each according to what he deserves, since judgment is the result of dominion. ﴿Those who did evil﴾ by going astray ﴿for what they did﴾, that is, because of it and in accordance with it, either through you, your swords, and the swords of your followers if I permit you to fight, or otherwise, by death from natural causes, through the angels striking their faces and their backs, and then by the punishment of the Hereafter for all their sins, without any of it being hastened for them in this world in a way that would diminish the punishment of the Hereafter. ﴿And He will reward﴾, that is, He will establish and honor ﴿those who did good﴾, that is, for their steadfastness in the religion, their patience upon it, and their endurance of the harm of their enemies, ﴿with the best﴾ (p-٦٧), that is, with the steadfastness which is at the furthest end of goodness, beyond which there is no end. For al-husna is the feminine form of al-ahsan (the best).

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 53, verse 32:

When He had promised those who did good, He described them, saying: ﴿Those who avoid major sins and immoralities﴾. That is, they exert themselves and strive hard to refrain from ﴿major sins (kaba'ir al-ithm)﴾, meaning those whose sinfulness the Lawgiver magnified after prohibiting them, by threatening punishment and prescribing the prescribed penalty (hadd). He joined to ﴿major sins﴾ His saying ﴿and immoralities (al-fawahish)﴾. The fahisha (immorality) is among the major sins: it is what the natural disposition finds repugnant, what the intellect denies, and what the sound nature finds loathsome.

When this restriction made clear that whoever falls into what is lesser, and what is lesser than that, is forgiven, He stated it explicitly, saying: ﴿Except (illa)﴾, that is, but ﴿the lapses (al-lamam)﴾ are pardoned. Whoever commits them does not leave the ranks of the good-doers. This is a disjunctive exception (istithna' munqati'), and perhaps He placed illa where lakinna ("but") would be, as an indication of a minor sin that may become a major one through the one who commits it treating it lightly, as He said, exalted is He: ﴿And you think it trivial, while it is with Allah tremendous﴾ [al-Nur: 15]. Al-lamam is the minor sins, and what is meant here is what occurs from them at times, as though it befell its doer as a slip without his choosing it, not what is adopted as a habit or multiplied until it becomes like a habit. Al-Razi said in al-Lawami': its origin is approaching a sin and then refraining from it before doing it. Dhu al-Nun said: mentioning immorality by one who knows God is like committing it by others. Ended. It is said: "alamma bi-l-makan" when one stays in a place only briefly. Al-Baghawi said: al-Suddi said: Abu Salih said that he was asked about al-lamam, and he said: it is the man who commits a sin and then does not return to it. He said: I mentioned that to Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, and he said: "A noble angel has indeed helped you against it." Then al-Baghawi said: the basic meaning of lamam and ilmam is what a person does from time to time, without repetition or persistence in it. Ended. On this basis, the exception may also be connected (istithna' muttasil).

Since kings do not forgive one whose offenses against them are repeated, even if they are small, the listener would find it great that the King of kings, glory be to Him, forgives the like of this, so He gave the reason by His saying: ﴿Indeed your Lord is of vast forgiveness﴾, that is, the One who has been good to you by sending you as a mercy to the worlds and lightening the burden on your community. ﴿He is of vast forgiveness (wasi‘ al-maghfira)﴾: He forgives minor sins as a right He made binding upon Himself, and He forgives major sins if He wills, unlike other kings, for if they wished to do so they would not be able to, and if they strove until they were able to do so at some time, their kingdom would be corrupted, leading to the loss or disruption of their rule.

When He described those who did good, and it might occur to someone that Allah knows them only by their deeds, and someone who acts upon the content of the verse might conclude that he is among the good-doers, He said, negating this: ﴿He knows you best﴾, that is, He knows your essences and conditions better than you know yourselves, ﴿when﴾ (idh) that is, at the time when ﴿He brought you into being (ansha'akum)﴾ originally ﴿from the earth﴾, whose nature is the nature of death: cold and dryness, through the creation of your father Adam, peace be upon him, from it, and the preparation of you for generation after you had no strength, near or remote, at all by which the good that suits your coming into being could be distinguished from what does not suit it. ﴿And when﴾ (idh) that is, at the time when ﴿you were embryos (ajinna)﴾, that is, hidden.

Since a human being may be in the belly of the earth, even though the fetus is known to the child in the womb, He clarified its meaning by His saying: ﴿in the wombs of your mothers﴾, after water and air were mixed with that cold, dry dust through it, and heat and moisture arose, so that these four humors became pure and base. But you have no knowledge at all; He knows at that time what you will become of good and evil, even if you act for a span of your life contrary to that, for He knows what He has disposed you towards of that, while you do not know except what is within yourselves, in a state in which you cannot encompass it with knowledge at that time.

Since it is customary for one who is free from sins to boast over one who has committed them, because of the love of boasting that man has been built upon, due to the deficiency with which he was created, and since his condition may change, so that the Book precedes against him and he becomes wretched, He based upon this His saying: ﴿So do not justify yourselves (fa-la tuzakku)﴾, that is, do not praise yourselves with purity (zakah), which is blessing and purity from baseness, ﴿yourselves﴾, that is, in reality, by one commending himself. For his commending himself is one of the signs of his being veiled from Allah, said al-Qushayri. Or figuratively, by one commending others among his brethren, for he often praises someone for something and then the opposite appears, and perhaps harm befalls him because of it. "Indeed a servant may act by the deeds of the people of Paradise until there is between him and it only a cubit or a forearm's length," the hadith. Therefore He gave the reason with His saying: ﴿He knows best﴾, that is, better than you and all creation, ﴿who is God-fearing (ittaqa)﴾, that is, one who strove against his soul until taqwa (God-consciousness) came to be in him. He will bring him beyond what he hopes for in reward in both abodes. How much more so one for whom taqwa has become a firm attribute.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 53, verse 33:

When He, glory be to Him, commanded him to turn away from the one who turned away from the honour of remembering the Most Great King and seeking refuge in Him, and forbade him from praising himself out of ignorance of the outcomes, and some people had apostatised from Islam, the cause of their apostasy was his (ﷺ) informing them of some of the great signs he had seen on the Night of the Isra' (the Night Journey). When the Surah of the Star (al-Najm) was revealed to him (ﷺ) and he (ﷺ) prostrated in it, the Muslims, the polytheists, the jinn and mankind all prostrated with him, as is related in al-Bukhari. No one among creation, not even the apostates, thought that they would turn back on their heels afterwards. On account of this, He said: ﴿Have you seen the one who turned away?﴾ That is, tell me about the one who ﴿turned away﴾ from Our remembrance after he had been eager for it, thinking, he and his people, that he was firmly established among his people through his faith and his deeds in the days of his faith.

﴿And he gave a little and then held back﴾. That is, he cut off that giving, despite its meagerness and scarcity, and nullified and spoiled it. He became like the digger who, in his digging, reached a hard rock (kudya). It is said of the well-digger: ajbal, when he reached a mountain, and akda, when he reached a kudya, that is, a great, very hard boulder upon which the axes have no effect. So he is unable with it to accomplish anything of his aim, and cannot penetrate it by any of his stratagems. Before that, when he encountered soft earth, he thought that nothing would prevent him from what he wanted. This is a reported, witnessed proof that no one among creatures has knowledge of what Allah has bestowed upon him in his own self, let alone upon others; so no one should declare himself or anyone else pure. It was said: it was revealed concerning al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, who embraced Islam and then apostatized because some of the polytheists reproached him, and because of his saying to him, "Return, and I will bear your punishment for you." It applies to everyone who openly apostatizes, or is hypocritical, or immerses himself in sins after (p-71) his faith, turning away from righteous deeds.

Since this matter, in which he had fallen into a grave peril of corrupting his deeds in the past and abandoning them in the future, so that he became in grave error regarding one of the two, is connected to the very foundation of the religion, namely disbelief and faith, and since no sensible person would do the like of this to himself except with insight, the Exalted said, rebuking him and reproaching him: ﴿Does he have knowledge of the unseen?﴾ That is, exclusively, ﴿of the unseen﴾, that is, all of it, such that no associate could share in it, and such that nothing of it could be hidden from him. ﴿So he sees﴾ that is, as a consequence of that, he ﴿sees﴾, that is, the complete seeing, so he knows all that benefits him and so he undertakes it, and all that harms him and so he avoids it, and he knows that this little that he gave has been accepted and that he is safe by it from ruin, so he is content with it.

When the dullard may suppose that the deeds of another benefit him, he expressed this, combining admonition and awe, with His saying: ﴿Or has he not been informed﴾, i.e., has he not been told with a great, continuous report, ﴿of what is in the scriptures of Musa﴾, i.e., the Torah attributed to him by its being sent down upon him, and likewise what follows it of the books of the prophets who came after him confirming it.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 53, verse 37:

When he (the author) had placed the Book of Musa, peace be upon him, first, because it is the greatest Book after the Qur'an, even though it is present among the people and can be consulted, he said: ﴿And Ibrahim﴾, and praised him with his words, using the doubled form of the verb to indicate the utmost fulfilment: ﴿who fulfilled﴾, meaning he completed everything he was commanded and everything he was tested with, and he was not disturbed by any anxiety whatsoever. He was the first to migrate from his people, and he endured the heat of the (intended) slaughter of his son, and likewise the heat of the fire, and he did not seek help from any created being. He singled out these two prophets because the claimants among the Children of Israel, the Jews (p-72) and the Christians, claim to follow Isa, peace be upon him, and among the Arabs they claim to follow Ibrahim, peace be upon him. As for everyone else, they have no firm basis, and no predecessor in a verified prophethood or a preserved law. Then he explained "who" (alladhi) in the Scrolls, or began a new statement with his words:

Verse 38 of Surah al-Najm: ﴿That no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another﴾. (Commentary text follows.)

Note: this translation of the commentary as given is as follows.

﴿Ala taziru﴾, that is, "does he not commit sin and bear [the burden]," ﴿wazirah﴾, that is, a soul that has reached a stage at which it is laden, ﴿wizra ukhra﴾, that is, its heavy load of sin. The meaning is that whoever bears another's sin, which is incumbent upon one of the two parties, must himself be sinful; and these two [states] are before turning away and after it.

When He negated that the sin of another could harm him, He then negated that the striving of another could benefit him, so He said: ﴿And that there is not for man﴾ whoever he may be ﴿except what he strives for﴾. Thus he must know the truth in whichever direction it lies, and then strive. The supplication of the believers for a fellow believer is part of his striving, through their affection for him, even if it is through their agreement with him in religion. Likewise, performing the Hajj on his behalf, giving charity and similar acts. As for a child, it is clear in this regard. As for what occurs due to knowledge and the like, it is the same. And the sacrifice of the Prophet (ﷺ) in his resolve is a great principle in this matter, for whoever follows him has indeed shown affection for him. This is a basis for giving charity on behalf of others and for gifting the reward of recitation and the like.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 53, verse 40:

Since it has been established that he has nothing except what he did, and nothing against him except what he did, and since in this world a person may do a thing, good or evil, without seeing it as done for its own sake or for anything else, he denied that the Hereafter is like this by saying: ﴿And that his striving﴾, i.e., whether of good or of evil, ﴿will soon be﴾, i.e., without any doubt, by a promise that admits no failure, even if the span of time is long, ﴿seen﴾.

And since the act of being shown (al-ittila', i.e., the disclosure itself) is in itself either praiseworthy or shameful, and not in relation to any specific individual, he made the verb passive (lil-majhul) by saying: ﴿will be seen﴾.

Since what is feared from it is recompense in general, not from a specific recompenser, He said: ﴿Then He will recompense him﴾. And since in this abode there may sometimes be leniency regarding some things and neglect of some of them, He said: ﴿with the fullest recompense﴾, meaning the most complete reward. If it is good, then it is with multiplication; and if it is other than that, then it is in equal measure for whomever God wills it for, and He pardons much. Yet it is a reminder to him.

When the sight of the deeds does not necessarily entail the sight of those who are entrusted with them, whether angels or others whom God has appointed for that task, and the more numerous the one who sees, the more terrifying the matter becomes, and the sight of the Greatest King is more fearful, He said, conjoining it to ﴿Nor shall a bearer of burdens bear the burden of another﴾, and making clear with particles of ultimacy that those who witness the deeds are many, owing to the multitude of His hosts, glory be to Him: ﴿And that to your Lord is the final end﴾, that is, to the One who has been good to you and no other, ﴿the final end﴾, that is, the ending by the return of creatures physically through resurrection and in meaning through deed and knowledge, and through the attribution of affairs and the sending forth of hopes, and the place of their return and its time, just as there was a beginning from Him. He emphasized this as a creation of all of that and a reckoning for it. Al-Baghawi narrated through the route of Abu Ja'far al-Razi, from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, may God be pleased with him, from the Prophet ﷺ, concerning this verse, that he said: "There is no reflection upon the Lord." He said: Similar to this is what was narrated from Abu Hurayrah, may God be pleased with him, as a raised (marfu') report: "Reflect upon the creation, but do not reflect upon the Creator, for reflection does not encompass Him." Abu Nu'aym narrated in al-Hilya from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both: "Do not reflect upon God, for you will never measure His measure." This is the intended meaning, and it is clear. So whoever interprets the verse by ittihad (unification of God with creation, a term of the mystics) or by other forms of deviation (ilhad), upon him is the curse of God, and upon the one who defends it and the one who remains silent about it.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 53, verse 43:

When the Exalted mentioned the voluntary matters (al-umur al-ikhtiyariyya) and placed them first, because they are the locus of trial, and He withdrew knowledge of them from their owners, and He warned of their consequence by His encompassing of everything, and the meaning of that is that He alone is the Able and He alone is the All-Knowing, He followed it with His saying, mentioning the involuntary matters (al-umur al-idtirariyya), which are at the utmost opposition, to complete the proof that He knows what is in souls without their owners and others, and that to Him is the final end, in return and in origination, He makes stand whatever He wills upon what He intends of the causes that are done by His permission, of laughter or weeping and other such contrary matters, which, were it not for habituation to them, a person would judge that one who is clothed in one of them is not clothed in its opposite at all. ﴿And that He﴾ And since the perceptual effects (al-ta'thirat al-idrakiyya) are referred to their causes, He emphasized the discourse concerning them, saying: ﴿He﴾, that is, none other than Him, ﴿causes to laugh and causes to weep﴾, that is, no one knows before the time of laughing or weeping that he will laugh or weep, nor that there will come to him what pleases him or saddens him. Were it said to him at the moment of laughter that after an hour he would weep, he would deny that. And perhaps what made him weep overtakes him while he is laughing, and the reverse.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 53, verse 44:

When death and life are more opposed to each other than what has passed, and the power to bring about both in one and the same person is at its greatest, and it might be attributed to one who kills, or who cures an illness, or who releases one who deserved to be killed, He emphasized, saying: ﴿And that He is the One﴾, i.e., not other than Him. And since the confusion is greatest in death, and death is most suited to weeping, and life is most suited to laughter, and the way of the scattered arrangement (al-nashr al-mushawwash) is more eloquent, He placed it first, saying: ﴿He causes to die and gives life﴾. And even if you see apparent causes, they carry no weight at all in reality; rather, it is He who created them.

Since the mention of giving life had come, and the classification of offspring into its two kinds was evident in its being specific to Him—indeed, it is utterly impossible for anyone other than Him—He left it without the kind of emphasis He had used in the preceding verse, and so He said: ﴿And that He created the pair﴾. Then He explained it with His words: ﴿the male and the female﴾, for if that were in the case of anyone else, it would have prevented daughters, since they are disliked by everyone. Then He mentioned what is evident and must be from His doing, so that the material of the two is one, and that is the water, which is the most mixable of things. So He said:

"from a drop of semen" — and He made the fact that it is from it clear by His saying: ﴿when it is emitted﴾, meaning, when it is spilled and gushed forth in actuality, not before that, so that there would be no room for objection that it was a beginning or something else. Rather, you know that the child is not created except after the emission has actually occurred. And its origin excluded what would allow any created being, by mere sight of it, to know whether it is suited for a female only, or for a male only, or for both, or whether it is ambiguous as to hermaphroditism.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 53, verse 47:

When He had presented these things as proof of the all-encompassing reach of His knowledge, it followed that they also indicate the perfection of His power. He concluded them with the first creation, and from this there necessarily follows the affirmation, with certainty, that He is able to resurrect. He expressed it in a way that implies that, since His promise has been announced through the tongues of all His messengers, it has become binding upon Him, in the sense that it must come to pass, because "the word is not changed with Him" (lā yubaddalu al-qawlu ladayh), and nothing other than that is meant. So He used the preposition of elevation (ḥarf al-isti'lā') for emphasis, as a rebuttal of their denial of it, and said: ﴿And that to Him [belongs] the creation of the next life﴾, meaning, specific to Him in knowledge and power. ﴿The nash'ah﴾, meaning the living existence, is read as a long vowel (mamdūd) by Ibn Kathīr and Abū 'Amr, and as a short vowel (maqṣūr) by the others; it is the verbal noun of nasha'a, meaning to bend, to bring up, and to make a sunnah (i.e., to originate a way). ﴿The other﴾, meaning the one by which creation is brought into being after He has caused them to die.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 53, verse 48:
