Since wealth and poverty are among the matters that lie between what is within one's choice and what is compelled, and each of the two has a cause, and since they are divided between females and males by a divine wisdom, such that the strength of the male does not benefit him in them and the weakness of the female does not harm her, and since the mention of the Last Creation was like an interruption, which only necessitated the mention of the First Creation, he followed the mention of both with it. The mention of wealth, although it implies poverty, is more fitting for bounty and for attribution to the Lord, and true wealth is only in that abode, so he delayed its mention and said: ﴿And that He﴾. And since it could be attributed to striving and other things, he emphasized it with the verb and said: ﴿He﴾, that is, alone, without regard to the striving of any striver or anything else, ﴿enriches﴾. And since true wealth is in fact the wealth of the soul, which is its contentment with what has been apportioned to it, its calm and its tranquility, and the owner of property is called rich only because property is that with which the soul becomes tranquil, whoever is content with all that God has apportioned is rich, and he is enriched in the Garden even if he was in this world. ﴿And grants sufficiency﴾, that is, He enabled him to possess property and made him content in all conditions. Al-Baghawi said: He gave him the principal of property and what is stored after sufficiency. He said: al-Akhfash said: "aqna" means "made poor." (End.) Al-Isbahani transmitted the like of it from Abu Zayd. So the hamza here is for removal (of the root sense), and it is said: "afnahu bi-kadha" meaning "satisfied him with such-and-such," and "aqnahu al-sadd" meaning "the obstruction enabled him to possess it."

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 53, verse 49:

When al-Shi'ra (Sirius) was singled out because it crosses the sky laterally, it was mentioned after the stars because the capacity to act by choice had been fully established, even though it is among the things that fall under that genus sworn by at the beginning of the surah. Because in its course it passes laterally over all the mansions by which the Arabs sought rain and to which they attributed the arrival of the wealth-bringing (or rain-bearing) asterism, it was worshipped apart from God by Abu Kabsha al-Khuza'i, since it was for him the most exalted of the stars. The Exalted said, emphasizing the foolishness of those who worship it: ﴿And that He is﴾, that is, none other, ﴿the Lord of al-Shi'ra﴾, that is, the one perfect in its meaning, which is passing over (al-'ubur). The people of astrology (ahl 'ilm al-nujum) say that the astrological judgments attributed to it are the most sound of what is attributed to the upper world. It is a star that shines behind al-Jawza' (Orion's belt constellation), and is called Kalb al-Jabbar (the Dog of the Mighty One). Al-Jawza' was named al-Jabbar by way of likening it to a king on his throne with a crown upon his head. Al-Razi said in al-Lawami': it is one of the two stars of the Lion's forelegs (dhira'ay al-Asad). Ibn al-Qass said in his book Dala'il al-Qibla: it is seen at the time of the dawn prayer, shining, its light exceeding the light of the other stars around it, and the dawn has obliterated the light of the rest of the stars. As for the other al-Shi'ra, it is al-Ghumaysa' (with a ghayn marked with a dot and a sad unmarked), and it is less bright than the first, and for this reason it was called al-Ghumaysa'. Al-Qazzaz said in his Jami': it was said that she wept over her sister until her eye became inflamed (ghamisat 'aynuha), meaning it became dim and vanished.

When God, Glorified is He, demonstrated the perfection of His knowledge and the all-encompassing scope of His power through the affairs of the two realms, the upper and the lower, this was a call to turn toward what pleases Him and a prohibition against approaching what angers Him. He then began to threaten whoever held back from that, citing what befell the fates of the earlier peoples as examples of His wondrous power, saying: ﴿And that He destroyed 'Ad﴾. He did not bring the pronoun of separation (ḍamīr al-faṣl, ضَمِيرَ الفَصْلِ) because no one claimed that anyone other than Him destroyed them. He magnified their matter by His saying (p. 78) ﴿the first﴾, meaning the most ancient in time, as an indication that He is the one who disposes of all times. He mentioned them first because the evil came upon them from the direction they had thought to be good, and they were certain that it came from the beneficial rain-bearing winds (al-anwā' al-nāfi'ah, الأنواء النافعة) whose rains they were accustomed to seeking. It has been said that 'Ad were two tribes: the first (al-ūlā, الأُولى) were the people of Hud, peace be upon him, and the second were Iram, possessors of pillars (Iram dhāt al-'imād). This was said by a group of scholars, among them al-Qushayri. Al-Baghawi said: They had descendants, and these became the second 'Ad. Ibn Jarir said: The first 'Ad are the ones God meant by His saying: ﴿Have you not considered how your Lord dealt with 'Ad?﴾ [al-Fajr: 6] ﴿Iram﴾ [al-Fajr: 7]. They were called the first 'Ad because the sons of Luqaym ibn Hazzal ibn Hazil ibn Anbal ibn 'Ad were, at the time God sent His punishment upon these people, residents of Makkah together with their brethren from the 'Amalekites, the sons of 'Imliq ibn Lawidh ibn Sam ibn Nuh, peace be upon him. So the punishment did not afflict them as it afflicted his people, who are the second 'Ad. Then they perished after some of them transgressed against others, and they annihilated one another. Other than Ibn Jarir said: Iram are the second 'Ad. He joined to them by conjunction His saying:

ّ**Thamud**: He destroyed them. Then he connected to the destruction His saying: ﴿So He left none remaining﴾, meaning, of the two groups, not a single one.

Whoever says that ʿAd are two tribes makes the non-survival specific to Thamud. The reading of ʿĀṣim, Ḥamzah and Yaʿqūb with *man ṣ-ṣarf* (non-declension of the name) is explicit that they are the people of Ṣāliḥ, peace be upon him; the reading of the rest with *ṣ-ṣarf* (declension) is more fitting to destruction and annihilation.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 53, verse 52:

When He mentioned first those whose destruction was by the very wind which is the source of the rains that come to them from the clouds, and followed them with those whose destruction by it was by its carrying them off to the Blast (al-sayha) and its terrifying them (p-79), He followed them with those whose destruction was by water, which is the ultimate end of the clouds, saying: ﴿and the people of Nuh﴾, that is, He destroyed them because of their wrongdoing in denying (the messengers). And since their destruction took place in a portion of past time, He said: ﴿from before﴾, that is, before the two groups. Thus in the speech there are two awe-inspiring elements that shake the heart and have an effect upon the soul: the description of these (people) as "the two tribes," and of those (people) as "the first." Had He not put them first, this would not have been. He gave as the cause of their destruction something that indicates there is no difference in His sight between strong and weak, or few and many, emphasizing this, because what is well known of the transgression of ʿAd necessitates that they were the most transgressive of people: ﴿Indeed they were﴾, that is, with the dispositions they had, which are like mountains from which there is no detachment, ﴿they﴾, that is, specifically, ﴿more wrongdoing﴾ than the two groups mentioned, ﴿and more transgressive﴾, that is, more excessive in going beyond bounds in wrongdoing, and more extreme in exceeding limits in sins, and more tyrannical and insolent, because the call of Nuh ʿalayhi al-salam persisted (against them), and because they were longer-lived and stronger in bodies. Along with that they were filling the earth. It is also permissible that the pronoun refers to the three groups.

Al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on Surah 53, verse 53:

When he had mentioned the destruction by the violent wind that arose from it, and then by the water that arose from the clouds that arose from the wind, he mentioned the destruction by wind, fire and water, to inform that He alone is the doer of what He wills of punishment from the elements that are the cause of life, both together and separately. So He said, placing the agent first, to inform of the specification of the punishment with what was mentioned, and to convey that He, exalted is He, is capable of everything, so He did not punish one group with what He punished the other with: ﴿And the overturned cities﴾, i.e., the cities turned over from their faces onto their backs, by a power which, because of its intensity and magnitude, made them as if they had overturned by themselves without any overturner. That is because He, glorified is He, split them from the earth, tearing them apart, then propelled them into the air up to the height of the sky, then turned them over, and followed them with stones of sulphurous fire, and overwhelmed them with water, the like of which is not found in the waters of this world. For this reason He said: ﴿He covered them﴾, i.e., He raised, lowered and brought down. So the bringing down was a true "covering," and the raising was figurative, because it was its cause. And they are the cities of the people of Lut, peace be upon him. He indicated the stones and the water with His saying, as a consequence of the covering and following upon it:

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 53, verse 54:

﴿So He covered them﴾, meaning: He made to follow them that which covered them, so that it was for them like a covering. He terrified them with His saying: ﴿what covered them﴾, meaning: a great matter of stones and other things, which the minds cannot contain in description. What He, glory be to Him, mentioned of the scriptures (ṣuḥuf) included the explanation of what benefits and what harms of deeds, and the explanation of monotheism (tawḥīd) through Allah, glory be to Him, encompassing the ultimate limits that have no limit beyond them, in knowledge and power, because of His particularity in explaining created things, and in explaining the resurrection (ba'th) as a warning of the deferred (al-ājil, the afterlife), and the destruction of those who apostatized as a warning of the immediate (al-ʿājil, this world), for one whose heart is averse to penetrating toward the deferred.

When He destroyed each one of these groups, so that none of its wicked ones remained, and saved those among them who obeyed Him, so that none of the obedient perished, and His destruction of each group was by something other than what destroyed the other group, each of these things pointed to the completeness of His knowledge and the perfection of His power. All that preceded in this surah of blessings and punishments was, because it was the most perfect form of judgment, a blessing to every believer, given what it contains of encouragement toward His reward and warning against His punishment. He addressed the head of the believers (ﷺ), since His address to him is more forceful in admonishing others, and said, making what has passed the cause of what follows: ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you dispute?﴾ That is, which gift of the One who does good to you, which is the source of all bounty and honour. It is a sign of knowledge of Him, like the shadow of a person in relation to the person, for just as a shadow cannot be conceived except for a person, so too is the act of the agent, and there is no effect without the one who effects. ﴿Tatamara﴾ means you doubt, by turning thoughts over in your mind concerning the desire to guide your people, to the point that you wish none of them to perish, although your Lord has decreed the destruction of many of them, in accordance with what His wisdom required. Some of your concern in that turning over was causing doubt in some [of your own thoughts]. When the discourse had been completed along this wondrous method and lofty style, in the finest eloquence, with admonitions, legislation, ancient stories and a great, complete warning, in a manner miraculous in many respects, it produced His saying, encouraging and warning, concluding the surah with what it began with, namely the mention of (ﷺ):

This is a warner (﴿هَذا﴾ the Prophet ﷺ, ﴿نَذِيرٌ﴾), that is, one who gives warning with great force. Since the messengers before him, upon them be prayer and peace, had their mission firmly established in souls, and hearts had settled into accepting it, such that it is not possible to deny it, he had informed about the denial of those who rejected them, the destruction of those who denied them, and the deliverance of the messengers and of those who believed them in support of them. There was no difference between him ﷺ and them in this, except that mercy toward him is more far-reaching and more prevailing, encouraging following him and warning against opposing him. He said: ﴿مِنَ النُّذُرِ الأُولى﴾, meaning: what was due to them is due to him, and you are like the earlier warners. So beware of what befell the deniers among them, and hope for what was granted to those who affirmed them.

Since every coming thing is near, and the Hour, which is what he warned of concerning the Resurrection and what lies before it, must come, because of the true promise made about it, adorned with proofs that admit no doubt in any way, there is then, in consideration of this, nothing nearer than it. He indicated this by the past tense form whose occurrence has been certain, and by the derivation of the active participle from the same root as the verb: ﴿The approaching one has drawn near﴾, meaning: the Hour that is near in itself, which was described to you as near by the verb many times, has drawn close, because it is the place where wisdom is fulfilled and greatness is manifested, and creation was made only for its sake; it includes the constriction and evil of life in the Resurrection, and everything that was promised to you in this world, through which this religion will become manifest and the corrupters will be suppressed.

When the noose tightened around mentioning it in this manner, the listener became eager for its refutation, so He resumed His speech with His words: ﴿There is none to disclose it﴾, and He added the qualification with His words: ﴿other than Allah﴾, meaning, whoever is lower in rank than the rank of the King who encompasses everything in power and knowledge, ﴿disclosing﴾, meaning, one who brings it into existence, establishes it, and makes its knowledge manifest, or who removes its distress and anxiety, even if he exerts himself greatly in the disclosing and in that effort. The ha' (taa' marbutah) here is for emphasis (mubalaghah). It is also permissible that it be a verbal noun (masdar), like al-jathiyah, al-kadhibah and al-baqiyah, in which case the ha' is for the feminine.

Since this has made clear that Allah alone unveils it (i.e., unveils its distress) for whomever He wills among His servants, and makes it heavy upon whomever He wishes, and unveils knowledge of its establishment (i.e., the Hour's appointed time), and no one else has any means whatsoever in any of that, He connected to this, and to the warning that preceded it, His saying, censuring and rebuking: ﴿Do you then marvel at this discourse?﴾ That is, at this great saying that comes to you in a continual manner according to events and needs. ﴿Do you marvel?﴾ in denial, and this is at the utmost degree of softening the hearts.

Since the one who is amazed may hold himself back from laughing, he made clear that they are not like that, and said: ﴿And you laugh﴾, i.e., in mockery, renewing this laughter of yours at it at every moment, while it is far from that. And since it only brings about sorrow by its being (p-83) he descended to sorrow and said: ﴿And you do not weep﴾, i.e., as is the due of one who hears it.

Since weeping may come from falling short in action, he made clear that the matter is graver than that, and said: ﴿and you﴾, meaning, while your state is that you are in your weeping, ﴿sāmidūn﴾, meaning persistent in work and striving in work, because the matter is serious. Persistence in work and earnestness in it at that time is therefore a cause of weeping. It is as if it were said: "Do not persist in work so that you weep." I only said this because *samada* (سَمَدَ) means: he persisted in work and raised his head in arrogance and rose up. *Samadati al-ibil* (سَمَدَتِ الإبِلُ) means the camels pressed on in travel and walked a severe pace. *Istamadda* (اسْمادَّ) means he swelled. *Sammada* (سَمَّدَ) means he stood bewildered, grieved, rejoiced, became heedless, was distracted, stood up, arrived, slept, became concerned, grew proud, was bewildered, became insolent, and was exultant. *Sammada al-arḍ* (سَمَّدَ الأرْضَ) means he made the land smooth, and also he put fertilizer (*al-sarqīn*, dung) in it. *Al-sha'r* (الشَّعَرَ) with *sammada* means he uprooted it. *Huwa laka samdan* (هو لَكَ سَمْدًا) means "it is yours perpetually" (*sarmadan*). *Al-sammīd* (السَّمِيدُ) means fine flour (*al-ḥuwwārā*). Al-Qazzāz in his *Jāmi'* and the author of *al-Qāmūs* mention this at length.

So the root, as you see, revolves around its spreading into persistence in work. Sometimes it refers to its originating motive that prompts it, sometimes to what arises from it, and sometimes to what lies between them, which is earnestness in work. The name thus applies to each of these sometimes literally, sometimes by metaphor of the first, and at other times by metaphor of the consequence. Intention is a motive, and likewise concern, standing, and raising the head arise from them, and that is its first sense.

*Al-sadam* (السَّدَمُ) means eagerness (*ḥirṣ*), concern, and being devoted to a thing. *Al-sadīm* (السَّدِيمُ) means thin mist, which is the beginning of unveiling. *Al-musaddam* (المُسَدَّمُ) means a neglected camel and one whose back is wounded, as if from removal. *Rakiyyatun sudm* (رَكِيَّةٌ سُدْمٌ) means a well gushing forth, because of the treatment in opening it, and because its gushing is persistence in work. Likewise *sadama al-bāb* (سَدَمَ البابَ) means he closed the door, i.e., sealed it. *Al-dasam* (الدَّسَمُ) means fat, because it energizes one to work and arises from it. *Al-wadak* and *al-wadar* and *al-danas* (الدَّنَسُ) mean filth. *Dasama al-maṭar al-arḍ* (دَسَمَ المَطَرُ الأرْضَ) means the rain moistened the land a little, because it is the beginning of much. *Al-qārūra* (القارُورَةَ): he sealed it. *Al-bāb*: he shut it, because one labors in opening it. *Al-dusma* (الدُّسْمَةُ) means dust tending toward blackness, as if it were the beginning of blackness. *Al-dasīm* (الدَّسِيمُ) is said of one whose parents are not of one kind, as if he were a beginning of each kind of them, and because mixing usually requires treatment. From it comes *al-dusma* for a base man, as if his kind were not complete in him, and because a thing's deficiency from its usual state requires treatment and deliberate action. *Al-daysam* (الدَّيْسَمُ) means one gentle in work and compassionate. *Ana 'alā dasmin min al-amr* (أنا عَلى دَسْمٍ مِنَ الأمْرِ) means I am at an edge of the matter. *Al-masad* (المَسَدُ), vowelled as *muḥarrakatan*, means the iron axle, because it is the tool of twisting, and a cord of palm fiber or doum-palm fiber, because it is the place of effort. *Al-misād* (المِسادُ) means a jar of ghee. *Damasahu* (دَمَسَهُ) means he buried it, and it may be both a beginning and an aim. From it comes *damasa baynahum* (دَمَسَ بَيْنَهُمْ), meaning he reconciled them, because he buried their grudges and worked at that. *Al-damṣ* (الدَّمْسُ) means concealing a thing and darkness, because it produces fatigue. *Damasa al-mawḍi'* (دَمَسَ المَوْضِعُ) means the place was effaced, from the fatigue of knowing it. *Damasa al-ihāb* (دَمَسَ الإهابَ) means he covered the hide in order to comb its hair. *Al-dams* (الدَّمْسُ) means a person, and vowelled with *tahrīk* it means what is covered. *Al-dūdamis* (الدُّودَمِسُ), with *ḍamma*, is a snake with swollen gills that blows and burns whatever it strikes with its breath, and among its effects arising from it is swelling.

Likewise, standing in bewilderment, heedlessness, joy, grief, play, sleep, pride, swaggering, elevation, and obstinacy. *Al-sammīd*, i.e., *al-ḥuwwārā*. *Al-samd* in the sense of *al-sarmad* (perpetual). *Al-samd* also means concern with regret, or anger with sorrow. *Al-dimās* (الدِّيماسُ) means shelter. Between these meanings lie *sammada al-arḍ*, *al-sha'r*, fierce travel, and earnestness in it, which is the very persistence. Likewise *al-sadīm* means one who remembers much, *mā'un musaddam* (ماءٌ مُسَدَّمٌ) and *'āshiq musaddam* (عاشِقٌ مُسَدَّمٌ) mean intensely loved, *al-dasīm* (الدَّسِيمُ) means the darkness of blackness, and also one who remembers much. *Dasama al-ba'īr* (دَسَمَ البَعِيرَ) means he daubed the camel with henna. *Al-masd* (المَسْدُ) means persistence of travel. Vowelled with *tahrīk*, *al-mamsūd* (المَضْفُورُ) means tightly braided and firmly twisted. *Rajulun mamsūd* (رَجُلٌ مَمْسُودٌ) means a man well-built in his frame, compared to it, and it takes the feminine with *ha'*. *Damasa baynahum* (دَمَسَ بَيْنَهُمْ) means he reconciled them, and this too comes from burying, because he buried their grudges.

Thus we clarify that taking *sumūd* in the verse to mean persistence in work is the better view, and that making the clause a circumstantial phrase (ḥāl) is preferable to making it coordinated with ﴿tadhakūn﴾ (laugh). That is the end of it, and God knows best.

When He urged them to prostrate, he explained it, as a consequence of the interrogation and what follows it, with His saying: ﴿So prostrate to Allah and worship [Him]﴾. That is: humble yourselves in great humility through the prostration of prayer, ﴿to Allah﴾, that is, the Supreme King; ﴿and worship﴾, that is, with every kind of worship, for indeed "﴿your companion has not strayed﴾ [al-Najm: 2]" from the command to that, "﴿nor has he erred﴾ [al-Najm: 2]."

Al-Razi said in al-Lawami': Imam Muhammad ibn Ali al-Tirmidhi said: "Our Lord has made us worship Him sincerely, that we should be to Him as servants, and that He should be to His servants as He is to them." End of quote.

If sujud were taken in the sense of frivolity (lahw), it would have been more appropriate to place it before "﴿you weep﴾" – and Allah knows best. It has become clear that its last part is the result of its first part, and its detailed part is the fruit of its connecting part. And Allah is the Guide.
